lessons.title: Read the difficulty before choosing a reading scaffold
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0010

CONTENT GOAL: Use contrasting observations to select a next instructional step for decoding, language comprehension, background knowledge or strategic reading while preserving access to grade-level text. LANGUAGE GOAL: Explain a reading-support decision with a text example, an observation and a limitation using because, although and a next-step question.

This is original synthetic instructional practice. Its worked explanations and guided checks are assisted study: no attempts or independent evidence are created by reading or mentally answering them. There is no learner diagnosis here. Language background does not establish ability, disability, culture traits or a preferred way of learning.

STAGE 1 - Locate the demand and gather different observations.
A reading failure does not identify its cause. Word recognition and fluency concern accurate, increasingly efficient access to print. Language comprehension includes vocabulary, clause relations and discourse references. Background knowledge concerns the concepts or context the author assumes. Strategic reading includes noticing a breakdown, rereading the relevant passage, asking a question and checking a proposed summary against the text. These demands can interact. Listen to a short reading, ask about meaning, inspect a difficult sentence and try a content check with less English demand. Compare observations rather than putting a learner in a permanent category. If word recognition is effortful, provide explicit foundational instruction while also developing oral vocabulary and listening and reading comprehension; S11 Recommendation 4 has Moderate evidence and does not reduce intervention to phonics alone. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Fluent words, missing relationship.
An original ecology sentence reads: 'Although the seeds reached both plots, only the fenced plot produced seedlings because grazing animals ate the new shoots outside it.' A synthetic reader pronounces the words accurately but says that seeds reached only one plot. This observation makes a missing concessive/causal relationship a useful next hypothesis; it does not prove that decoding never needs attention. The teacher marks what although contrasts, traces it to the fenced plot and asks the reader to connect because with the loss of shoots. They sketch the two plots, reread the exact sentence and revise a summary. Counterexample: repeating isolated letter sounds for the entire lesson supplies no instruction in the relationship that this observation exposed. A later independent sentence would be needed before making a claim about transfer. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted, no evidence.
A learner can point to the protected seedlings in a diagram but misreads 'outside it.' What would you inspect next? Worked guidance: ask the learner to locate the referent of it in the sentence and explain the diagram-text connection. The diagram gives partial content evidence, not proof of reading comprehension. If the learner also cannot explain the role of grazing with a familiar-language discussion or visual demonstration, build that background concept. If the learner knows the relation but keeps a contradictory summary without checking, model monitoring and rereading. Do not infer a disability or fixed ability from any of these observations.

STAGE 2 - Start from observed literacy resources.
For an L1-literate reader, invite an account of how they monitor understanding, summarize and use headings in a familiar language. Those resources may support English reading. Examine differences between known and new writing systems and sound-symbol relationships; use contrastive phonics where observations warrant it. Do not assume every English sound, spelling pattern or genre convention transfers unchanged. For a learner who is not yet literate in any language, do not presume a print strategy that has not been learned. Teach print concepts, phonological awareness, phonics, word recognition and fluency as needed alongside a rich oral-language foundation and meaningful encounters with text. Both learners still need intellectually worthwhile content and comprehension development. Prior literacy information must come from respectful inquiry and observed work, not nationality. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Two entry points into one history text.
A class reads a demanding informational account of a community building. Reader A summarizes familiar-language accounts effectively but needs support with English vowel patterns and references such as 'the former site.' The teacher connects A's existing summary strategy to the new account, compares relevant print patterns and models the reference. Reader B has not yet learned to read in a familiar language. The teacher pairs images and oral discussion of a building with explicit print-to-speech work on selected words, then supports shared reading of a meaningful passage. Both learners discuss what changed and revisit the source text. Counterexample: starting both at letter naming solely because both are ELs ignores A's resources; asking B to transfer an unlearned print strategy ignores B's instructional needs. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]

STAGE 3 - Teach genre and strategy in the actual text.
A narrative may organize events around characters and change; a lab report organizes a question, methods, observations and an interpretation. Teach how these arrangements guide a reader's purpose. A random list of technical nouns cannot explain why an observation section differs from an explanation. With a report, model a think-aloud: 'I will scan the heading to locate observations, read the sentence closely, and check whether the explanation claims more than those observations show.' Skimming establishes an overview; scanning locates a needed item; close rereading tests meaning. Choose the strategy for the purpose, then invite the reader to explain whether it helped. S12 is the 2008 adolescent-literacy guide, not EL-specific research. Its discussion of explicit vocabulary and comprehension strategy instruction can inform planning, but it does not establish an EL-specific causal effect. Pair its bounded contribution with S11 rather than claiming a guaranteed effect or timeline. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S12 source.obj0010-0013.s12.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted, no evidence.
A scientific paragraph is difficult. One plan permanently replaces it with an easy summary. A second plan chunks the original at meaningful boundaries, supplies a small glossary and a visual, and uses partner reading before students reconnect the chunks and explain the original. Worked guidance: choose the second plan, then check whether learners can connect the chunks. A summary can orient or supplement; it cannot become the sole permanent curriculum. Retain the grade-level conceptual target and return to the full passage. A partner's explanation is useful assistance, not the learner's independent reading evidence. [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

STAGE 4 - Observe, adjust and preserve literacy work.
Use a short oral prediction or whiteboard sketch to make an initial idea visible. Require actual reading next, followed by a written explanation anchored to the text. Oral entry does not substitute for reading and writing. Ask what each observation can show: accurate word reading, a causal interpretation, knowledge of the concept or use of monitoring. Change support responsively and offer a fresh passage for later independent checking; no fixed fading schedule is implied. This slice samples reading decisions and two genres. It does not reproduce exact Massachusetts Standard 10 grade bands, prescribe a reading program, establish disability, or cover the complete range of literary and informational texts. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

lessons.title: Use reading, drafting and responsive feedback to develop writing
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0011

CONTENT GOAL: Design a content-anchored writing sequence with reading, planning, drafting, feedback and revision, drawing on observed first-language resources. LANGUAGE GOAL: Explain how a specific language choice improves a written claim, evidence link or organization, and justify one responsive feedback move.

All examples are original and synthetic. The guided checks are assisted study and create no attempts or independent evidence. Reading this lesson, copying its model or revising with its guidance is not independent mastery. Feedback addresses observable writing and instructional next steps; it never infers ability, disability or culture traits from a language label.

STAGE 1 - Read as a writer, write as a reader.
Select a passage whose organization serves the content goal. Have students read it for meaning before analyzing how its author connects claims and details. Annotation can expose a misunderstanding: a learner who labels an observation as a cause needs to reread the evidence, not simply add a transition word. Short written questions and summaries can focus a subsequent reading. Reading then supplies ideas and language for writing; writing makes an interpretation inspectable and prompts further reading. Keep a learner's original draft available when discussing a revision so that the learner can explain what changed. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Feedback changes a relationship.
In an original class source, 'A roof covered the west wall. The east wall remained exposed. After the storm, the paint on the west wall was dry, while water marked the east wall.' A synthetic first draft says, 'The roof stopped all damage.' The teacher first responds to the content overclaim: 'Your source describes water and paint on two walls. Which quoted observation supports all damage?' The learner rereads and drafts, 'The covered wall was dry after this storm, while water marked the exposed wall.' Next the teacher models how while connects the comparison and asks the learner to preserve the limit 'after this storm.' This is responsive feedback on meaning and a useful language structure, not an indiscriminate correction of every surface error. Counterexample: fixing punctuation while accepting all damage leaves the scientific claim unsupported. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted, no evidence.
Should the teacher write the entire final paragraph for the learner? Worked guidance: model one relevant relationship, give an organizer for evidence and limits, and ask the learner to draft and explain the next revision. A model can make a choice visible; replacing the learner's composition hides what the learner can do. Preserve the original answer in the practice system and use a later attempt for a fresh response. Do not call a supported revision unaided evidence.

STAGE 2 - Plan a process with a purpose for each support.
Begin with a content question and a real audience. Read, gather relevant examples, and use a graphic organizer that matches the genre. An explanation organizer might separate claim, evidence and connection; a narrative organizer might track situation, events and change. Invite familiar-language notes, sketches and partner talk when they help the writer develop ideas. Draft in the target genre, confer about an important next step, revise ideas and organization, then edit selected conventions. The sequence may loop back to reading or planning when a gap appears. Process writing is not merely assigning a first draft and then grading the same text as final. Language supports should help entry and continued development; do not leave an identical template as a permanent ceiling. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

STAGE 3 - Use L1 writing and rhetorical knowledge as a bridge.
Ask what the learner already does when making an argument, reporting an event or addressing an audience in a familiar language. Compare an actual piece of writing or an explanation of choices with the purpose of the new assignment. A familiar-language outline may already organize reasons and supporting examples. A writer might deliberately delay a claim for a particular audience; discuss how a current school genre signals its purpose and where that claim might help this audience. This is inquiry into choices and conventions, not a claim that every writer from a language or culture organizes text the same way. Make expectations explicit while respecting the writer's repertoire. Do not treat all L1 patterns as errors or demand that learners abandon them. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Genre, audience and a bridge.
A synthetic student has prepared a familiar-language account of a family garden for relatives. For a school exhibition the student must write an informational label explaining how a seed bank preserves varieties. The teacher asks the student to explain the sequence in the account, then compares it with an informational model: define the seed bank, explain storage, and connect it to preserving varieties. The student uses a bilingual outline to carry ideas forward and decides which personal detail serves the new audience. A short conference targets references that make stored seeds and plant varieties clear. Counterexample: attributing the first organization to a national trait would replace evidence about this writer with a stereotype. Another counterexample is merely translating the account word for word without teaching the new genre's purpose. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted, no evidence.
A learner explains a source confidently on a whiteboard. Is extended writing unnecessary? Worked guidance: the oral explanation offers a useful entry and content observation. Ask the learner to reread the source, draft a short evidence-based account, then develop a connected explanation through feedback and revision. Oral fluency does not demonstrate written discourse, control of reference across paragraphs or independent reading. Listen for the idea and inspect the writing separately. A transcript copied from a partner is also not independent writing. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

STAGE 4 - Name the evidence level honestly.
S11 is the 2014 WWC English-learner practice guide for elementary and middle school. Recommendation 3, on structured opportunities to develop written language skills, carries a Minimal evidence rating. Its suggested content-anchored assignments, language supports, peer collaboration and constructive feedback are useful planning guidance; the rating must not be relabeled Strong or treated as a guarantee that any scaffold causes a particular gain. S11 Recommendations 1 and 2 have Strong evidence, but those ratings do not transfer automatically to Recommendation 3. Use local observations to adjust a lesson while keeping the research limitation visible. Do not invent a timeline, effect size or causal claim for these examples. [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

STAGE 5 - Observe a next step without reducing writing to correctness counts.
Read for whether the draft answers its content question, supports a claim and guides its audience. Give a specific acknowledgment, identify a consequential gap and request a revision that the writer can explain. If a relationship is clear but a tense form is inconsistent, teach that form in context; if the relationship is absent, grammar correction alone cannot supply it. Keep content and language goals connected but inspect both. Later offer a fresh related task with supports appropriately reduced and record any remaining assistance. This lesson samples informational writing and revision. It does not supply a full grade-band conventions progression, every literary genre or a universal feedback schedule. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

lessons.title: Plan and assess content and language together
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0012

CONTENT GOAL: Preserve a demanding disciplinary target while planning accessible text work and distinguish evidence of content understanding from English form. LANGUAGE GOAL: Pair a content objective with an observable language objective, connect each to an assessment observation, and explain a scaffold using text evidence.

The classroom situations here are original and synthetic. Guided checks provide assisted explanations and create no attempts or independent evidence. These examples are not official Massachusetts standards wording or an official test item. They illustrate planning decisions; a teacher must select the applicable Massachusetts curriculum framework and grade-level standard for the actual lesson.

STAGE 1 - Begin with the disciplinary work and its language.
Identify what learners must understand or do in the content area, then inspect the language needed to participate. The Massachusetts content frameworks and WIDA ELD Standards work in tandem; neither objective replaces the other. In a history comparison, students may need to compare two accounts and explain how each supports a claim. Their language work includes attributing an account, comparing details and qualifying a conclusion. Merely listing English vocabulary beside a content topic does not establish an aligned objective pair. Specify observable performance and collect evidence for both. A WIDA English language proficiency score describes ELP, not content ability, intelligence or disability. It is one planning input alongside classroom observations and knowledge of the learner's resources. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Two goals and two observations.
An original social-studies lesson asks students to compare a town map with a resident's account of a public square. Content objective: explain one supported change in the square and one uncertainty about its use. Language objective: orally compare two details using source attribution, then write a connected explanation with a contrast and a qualification. The teacher provides an enlarged map, a few contextual explanations and a reference chart for phrases such as 'the map shows' and 'the account suggests.' During discussion the teacher records whether the comparison is supported; in writing the teacher checks whether the attribution and qualification communicate that reasoning. Counterexample: counting uses of however while accepting unsupported claims checks a form but not the content objective. A clear claim communicated with emerging English still supplies useful content evidence, while needing continued language instruction. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted, no evidence.
A learner misreads a dense English question about where a building stood, then accurately connects the map symbols and the building location during a low-language demonstration. Does this establish inability to learn history? Worked guidance: no. The contrast points to a language/access demand worth investigating. Ask the learner to connect a specific phrase in the question to the map and explain the evidence with support. Retain the history target. The demonstration is partial content evidence and does not prove that the learner has read the account independently. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

STAGE 2 - Analyze authentic text before choosing supplementary materials.
Authentic content-area texts carry a real disciplinary purpose and often compress meaning through specialized words, dense noun phrases, reference chains and genre conventions. Before a lesson, locate a sentence whose meaning matters to the objective. Decide what background context, vocabulary or visual would unlock that relationship. First-language materials, images and brief supplementary readings can build access; they must lead learners back to the main text. Chunk at meaningful boundaries and ask learners to reconnect the argument. Permanent replacement of the grade-level passage with a simplified summary abandons part of the target. This module's invented excerpts are transparent rehearsal materials for those planning decisions, not artifacts masquerading as authentic historical sources. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - A science text stays central.
For planning rehearsal, consider this original sentence: 'Because reeds slow moving water, particles can settle among their stems; however, this process does not remove every dissolved substance.' A class target is to explain what the described process can and cannot do. The teacher uses a labeled sketch of stems and particles, previews settle in context and chunks the sentence at the semicolon. Partners then reconnect because and however, reread the full sentence and write an explanation with a limit. For a real lesson, the teacher would use an appropriate authentic science text and check its exact claims. Counterexample: assigning only a plant-coloring page may be accessible but supplies no evidence about the process or its limitation. Another counterexample is accepting a perfectly grammatical claim that reeds remove everything. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted, no evidence.
One learner writes 'Reeds slow water, particles down, not all substances.' Another writes 'Reeds remove every substance because they are green.' What next? Worked guidance: the first response contains a potentially useful content distinction and needs a probe plus language support to connect its ideas. The second is more conventionally formed but contradicts the passage and gives an unsupported cause. Request source evidence from both, teach the missing relation or language as appropriate, and keep the standards-based content expectation. Do not convert English form into a proxy for science understanding. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

STAGE 3 - Make an oral entry lead into literacy.
A whiteboard claim and partner explanation can reveal an idea and make revision possible. Give the listener a task: ask which textual detail supports the explanation or which limit remains. Then require actual reading of the main passage and writing that develops the explanation across connected sentences and, over time, extended discourse. Oracy is a bridge into literacy, not permission to omit it. S11 Recommendation 2 supports integration of oral and written English into content-area instruction. It does not certify mastery from one successful conversation. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

STAGE 4 - Assess the construct and adjust access.
Ask separately: did the learner make a defensible content claim; did they use the intended language to communicate it; and what assistance was present? A labeled model may reduce unnecessary English demand while preserving a conceptual comparison. If the target itself is reading a complex source, however, replacing all reading with the teacher's explanation changes that target. State what an observation does and does not show. Use the evidence to reteach a concept, unpack a clause, adjust a glossary or offer further practice. Do not assign low content expectations from an ELP level, a home language or a grammar error. No assessment here infers ability, disability or culture traits. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

STAGE 5 - Review the alignment.
Check that the lesson names a real content demand, a language function serving it, access supports, student interaction, text engagement and evidence for each objective. Consult the applicable Massachusetts framework and WIDA 2020 materials for the actual grade and domain; this slice does not quote a grade-specific standard that was not supplied. It samples social-studies and science reasoning, not every discipline or a full standards progression. Keep supplementary materials subordinate to the learning purpose and revise support from observations rather than a fixed English-proficiency ceiling. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

lessons.title: Analyze one mentor text and read the holistic rubric responsibly
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0013

CONTENT GOAL: Build a coherent mentor-text analysis, distinguish the public Part I shape from original later practice parts, and explain what a provisional holistic judgment can support. LANGUAGE GOAL: Support an instructional decision with a literal mentor quotation, a language analysis and a reason connecting the support to the goal.

These worked examples and guided checks are assisted study. They create no attempts or independent evidence. The app's five-part practice is original and unofficial. It is not an official MTEL prompt, a live exam form, an official scoring service or a claim of complete SEI competence. No official sample mentor text or official sample response is reproduced here.

STAGE 1 - Know what the public materials actually provide.
The public S2 study guide and S3 practice test provide a sample for Part I only. Part I asks the candidate to identify the grade-level cluster and relevant secondary discipline, set a content objective, identify essential Tier One, Tier Two and Tier Three vocabulary, analyze sentence-level and discourse-level features, and state three language objectives addressing vocabulary development and oracy, reading comprehension and written discourse. The analysis uses specific examples from the selected mentor text. The same mentor must serve all five parts, and Part I(a) must identify it for the responses to be scored under the public directions. This describes the public task shape, not a reproduction of its full wording. Consult S2 at https://www.mtel.nesinc.com/Content/StudyGuide/MA_SG_CRI_56.asp for the published material. Official wording of live Parts II-V is not supplied; this app labels each invented later part original, unofficial practice. [S2 source.rubric.2026-11-08] [S3 source.obj0010-0013.s3.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Analyze a short original passage, then tie goals to it.
For assisted illustration only: 'The committee kept the damaged map because its notes identified paths that newer maps omitted. Although the ink was faded, the map helped residents compare earlier routes with today's streets.' Content goal: explain why a damaged record can still contribute historical evidence. Possible vocabulary choices include map as everyday Tier One, compare as broadly useful Tier Two, and a discipline-specific discussion of historical evidence rather than inventing a technical word absent from this passage. A tier is a context-sensitive instructional choice; do not force every text to contain every tier. At sentence level, because links preservation to evidentiary value and although signals a concession. At discourse level, the second sentence develops the reason in the first through a contrast between earlier and current routes. A vocabulary/oracy objective asks partners to use compare when discussing the quoted routes; a reading objective asks learners to explain the concession with a quotation; a written-discourse objective asks for a connected explanation of the map's value and limitation. Counterexample: naming conjunctions without explaining their meaning does not analyze the passage. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S2 source.rubric.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted, no evidence.
A candidate analyzes this map passage in Part I but plans reading support for an unrelated plant passage in Part III. Is a good activity enough? Worked guidance: no. The same-mentor rule requires coherent work on the declared text throughout. In the app's original practice, return to the bound mentor, quote its exact words in every part and justify how each support serves the identified objectives. The new community-archive mentor is an authored practice passage, not the official sample; this short map illustration is not a substitute for that task's bound text. [S2 source.rubric.2026-11-08] [S3 source.obj0010-0013.s3.2026-11-08]

STAGE 2 - Read the existing official rubric as holistic.
The existing version rubric.mtel56.public@1 preserves the public performance characteristics: Purpose, Subject Matter Knowledge, Support and Rationale, together with the holistic 1-4/U/B scale. The characteristics inform one judgment; they are not four numeric analytic subscores and have no invented weights. Apply U/B gates before considering 1-4: B denotes no response; U includes an unrelated, illegible, primarily non-English, insufficient-length or merely repeated-assignment response under the public descriptions. These are response classifications, not judgments of a person's intelligence or worth. Do not invent a minimum word threshold. For a scoreable response, compare the whole response with the holistic descriptors, name missing evidence and acknowledge uncertainty. [S2 source.rubric.2026-11-08] [S3 source.obj0010-0013.s3.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Criterion feedback is evidence, not an analytic score.
An original candidate sentence says, 'Partners will discuss the passage, and then they will write.' A useful comment under Support is: 'The phrase "discuss the passage" does not identify a mentor detail or a demand that the discussion addresses. Quote a sentence and explain what partners will notice.' Under Rationale, ask why that noticing prepares the later written explanation. This feedback identifies an observable omission and a next step; it does not turn four comments into four numbers. A later reviewer may propose one provisional holistic score with clear limits, but may not claim to be the official MTEL scorer. Counterexample: deriving an average from invented criterion numbers creates a scoring system absent from the public rubric. [S2 source.rubric.2026-11-08] [S3 source.obj0010-0013.s3.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted, no evidence.
What can be concluded when one practice part is missing and mentor evidence is ambiguous? Worked guidance: state the missing part and ambiguity, inspect U/B applicability first and compare only the available response to the holistic descriptions. Any proposed holistic score stays provisional and needs review; no calibrated probability or automatic mastery follows. If a learner disputes a judgment, compare quoted evidence and the descriptors again and seek a human mentor's review rather than averaging invented subscores. [S2 source.rubric.2026-11-08] [S3 source.obj0010-0013.s3.2026-11-08]

STAGE 3 - Keep the existing writing workflow honest.
The writing workspace saves an immutable attempt with its task version, mentor text identity and hash, and rubric binding. It creates no automatic score or independent evidence. Review proceeds through the existing manual or Grok handoff packet/proposal workflow; this lesson makes no AI call. A proposal can contain comments grounded in literal candidate quotations and mentor anchors plus one provisional holistic score. Human review requires a real human action. Completion, a source_checked label, a copied model or a model-only reviewEvent does not confer independent evidence. Use the same mentor in all five parts and preserve the original answer when corrections or review events are added.

STAGE 4 - Connect exam scope with endorsement and classroom practice.
Under the supplied 603 CMR 7.14 snapshot, the SEI Teacher Endorsement may be awarded through a Department-approved course of study, a Department-approved assessment, approved degree training, an ESL/ELL license, or an approved equivalent out-of-state credential, subject to the regulation's conditions. Field 56 is one approved assessment pathway, not all SEI competence. The rule connects knowledge and skills to 7.08(3)(a)-(e) and 7.14(1)(b): planning for linguistically diverse learners, accessible content, social and academic language, safe collaborative high expectations, family partnership, reading/writing, oral language, assessment and academic vocabulary. Endorsements do not constitute educator licenses. Passing an exam does not certify complete classroom competence forever or replace ongoing professional practice. These are bounded crosswalk points from the supplied 2026-11-08 packet, not individualized licensure advice. [S7 source.obj0010-0013.s7.2026-11-08] [S8 source.obj0010-0013.s8.2026-11-08]

STAGE 5 - Integrate, then name remaining gaps.
For one text, align a content objective, language analysis, supports for reading and writing, structured interaction and assessments that distinguish content reasoning from English control. Keep grade-level rigor and check the reasoning behind each choice. S11 Recommendation 3 retains its Minimal writing-evidence rating even in a polished plan. This slice does not supply non-public Parts II-V, all ten live mentor texts, secret keys or benchmark papers beyond the published material. Its narrow practice does not complete Objective 0013 or the objectives it references. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Locate a reading breakdown beyond word recognition
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative scenario, not an official examination item. A grade 7 reader pronounces a habitat passage accurately but interprets "Although the pond refilled, the nesting birds did not return" as saying that the birds returned. Which next teaching move best fits this observation?

options.text: Restart the entire lesson with isolated letter naming because English reading difficulties always begin there.
Unpack the contrast signaled by although, connect each clause to a sketch, and reread to check the interpretation.
Accept accurate pronunciation as sufficient proof that the passage was understood.
Remove causal and contrastive relationships from all future texts for this reader.

answerKey.feedback: The move targets the concessive relationship while keeping the passage and checks a revised interpretation. Fluent word reading alone neither establishes comprehension nor rules out other needs. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: The observed error concerns a clause relationship. Foundational skills deserve attention when evidence warrants it, but an automatic letter-naming restart misses this specific meaning demand. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Accurate pronunciation is one observation about reading. The contradictory paraphrase still requires instruction and a meaning check; pronunciation cannot stand in for comprehension. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Permanent removal of relationships lowers the reading demand. A responsive scaffold should make this relationship accessible and return the learner to the original text. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Separate a language demand from a content claim
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative scenario, not an official examination item. A learner cannot answer a dense English question about a food chain but correctly shows the same feeding relationships with labeled organisms and explains them in a familiar language. What is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Conclude that the learner cannot learn the science concept and permanently replace the standard.
Ignore the demonstration because only conventionally written English can show science understanding.
Declare both independent English reading and science mastery established by the demonstration.
Use the content demonstration as partial evidence, investigate the English demand, and teach access to the original question while retaining the science target.

answerKey.feedback: The response separates evidence of the concept from access to English and keeps the science demand. WIDA ELP information describes language proficiency, not content ability. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: The demonstration supplies relevant content evidence, so permanent reduction of the science expectation is not justified. The contrast calls for inquiry into language and access. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: English form is not the whole content construct. Dismissing a meaningful demonstration loses evidence that can guide rigorous instruction and more precise language support. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Build from demonstrated first-language literacy
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative scenario, not an official examination item. A grade 6 reader uses headings and summarizes an informational text successfully in a familiar language. In English, some sound-symbol patterns and references cause difficulty. Which plan uses the observed resources?

options.text: Connect the existing summary and heading strategies to English text, teach relevant contrastive phonics and references, and check comprehension.
Ignore prior reading and require a complete restart at letter naming for all EL readers.
Assume that every sound-symbol relationship and genre convention transfers unchanged.
Provide oral discussion indefinitely while withholding all English print until speech is fluent.

answerKey.feedback: The plan transfers observed strategies while explicitly teaching differences that matter in English. First-language literacy is a resource, not proof that every English pattern is already known. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.c: Transfer can support reading, but writing systems, spelling patterns and conventions can differ. The observed English difficulties call for targeted instruction and checking. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Oral language supports literacy, but it is not a prerequisite ceiling that excludes meaningful print. Coordinate oral development, English print instruction and comprehension. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Plan an initial literacy entry point

Treat the absence of print literacy as proof of low conceptual ability and remove history content.
Build an oral-language foundation and explicit initial print skills alongside supported reading and meaningful history content.
Assign only oral conversation for the year and postpone all reading and writing instruction.

wrongFeedback.b: Print literacy history does not establish conceptual ability. The oral ideas show resources to build on while maintaining a worthwhile content target and explicit literacy teaching. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S11 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Read a lab report differently from a narrative
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative scenario, not an official examination item. After reading a fictional adventure, students approach a lab report as a sequence of exciting events and cannot distinguish observations from interpretation. Which instruction best addresses the problem?

options.text: Preteach a long list of unrelated technical nouns and leave the report organization unexplained.
Compare the purposes and organization of narrative and lab report, model how headings separate method, observation and interpretation, and read for each purpose.
Teach that all texts have an identical structure so one summary template always fits.
Give only a teacher summary of the experiment and stop asking students to read the report.

tasks.title: Chunk text without changing the curriculum ceiling

tasks.title: Make feedback part of writing development
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative scenario, not an official examination item. A student drafts a museum explanation that claims every old photograph is reliable evidence. Which response best uses reading and writing together?

tasks.title: Align and inspect both objectives

wrongFeedback.b: An isolated form exercise is not evidence that learners can communicate the targeted historical comparison. Language objectives should serve the content purpose. [S1 source.framework.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S13 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Carry an oral entry into reading and writing

tasks.title: Keep the mentor constant across five practice parts

tasks.title: Keep the writing recommendation's evidence rating intact
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative scenario, not an official examination item. A team uses the 2014 WWC English-learner guide to plan content-anchored writing, peer talk, language supports and constructive feedback. How should it characterize Recommendation 3?

tasks.title: Investigate different barriers in a harbor account
tasks.prompt:
Original unfamiliar non-math application. All people, observations and passages are synthetic. This is not an official examination item or official writing prompt. There is no deterministic answer key or keyword grading. The response remains needs_review and provisional/manual pending a real human judgment.

A grade 6 class reads an informational account of changes to a small harbor:

'Before the footbridge opened, residents crossed the channel in a ferry. Although the bridge made walking across possible, the ferry continued to carry supplies that were too heavy for the narrow bridge. The council kept the landing so that those deliveries could continue. A later photograph shows an empty landing, but it cannot establish that no deliveries occurred at other times.'

The content goal is to explain why two crossing routes coexisted and what the photograph cannot establish. Reader A reads the passage accurately aloud but says the bridge ended every ferry journey. A successfully summarizes familiar-language accounts and uses headings to find information. Reader B has not yet learned to read in any language but, during an oral discussion with a sketch, proposes that people and heavy supplies might need different routes. Reader C recognizes the English words but asks what a ferry and a landing are; after a picture-based explanation C can connect them. These observations are limited, not fixed learner profiles. A colleague proposes giving all three learners only a permanently simplified caption.

Develop and justify a responsive sequence:
1. Quote a clause that could explain A's misunderstanding. Distinguish a decoding observation from language-comprehension, background-knowledge and strategic-monitoring hypotheses. Identify an additional observation that could change your interpretation rather than declaring a diagnosis.
2. Explain how you would use A's demonstrated L1 literacy while teaching relevant English demands. Contrast that entry with explicit initial print instruction and oral-language support for B. Keep the same meaningful content question without assuming an unlearned transfer strategy.
3. Build the specific background knowledge C needs and check whether it helps C interpret the passage; do not equate knowing a label with understanding the relation.
4. Model a purposeful reading strategy, such as checking a summary against although or tracing those deliveries. Explain how the informational organization differs from a narrative of one ferry trip.
5. Chunk the original, choose a visual or glossary support, and require reconnection and rereading. Explain why a permanently simplified caption as the sole curriculum would lose the goal.
6. Specify a short oral entry, actual text reading and written explanation, then a later fresh check with assistance recorded. Identify what each observation can show and what remains uncertain.

Use the bounded S1 reading scope, S10's language-resource framing and S11's combination of foundational, vocabulary and comprehension instruction. If using S12 to justify explicit strategies, state that it is the older 2008 adolescent-literacy guide, not EL-specific causal evidence.

Review boundary: evaluate reasoning, quotations, support choices and uncertainty through a real human action. There is no single required plan or keyword list. Completion, unfamiliarity and a source_checked label do not establish independent evidence or mastery. Do not infer ability, disability or culture traits from English proficiency, language background or any isolated response.

tasks.title: Develop a museum label through reading and revision

A grade 7 class is preparing an informational museum label about a community seed collection. The original source passage says:

'Volunteers stored seeds from several gardens in labeled envelopes. The labels recorded where the seeds were collected and when. These records help later gardeners compare varieties, but a label alone cannot show how well a plant will grow in a different garden. The collection preserves choices for future planting; it does not guarantee that every seed will sprout.'

A synthetic first draft reads, 'The collection guarantees plants everywhere. They wrote names so everything is safe.' The writer can orally explain in a familiar language that a record preserves information, and has previously written an organized personal account for relatives. The learner wants the museum audience to understand the collection's purpose. A peer suggests adding more technical words without revisiting the source. Another adult proposes correcting every English form and supplying a complete replacement paragraph.

Create and justify a writing sequence:
1. Quote the draft and source to identify a content misunderstanding, an unclear reference and an organizational need. Explain how writing can reveal a reading problem and how rereading can support revision.
2. Use respectful inquiry into the learner's existing L1 writing choices. Describe a bridge from the personal account to an informational label for a new audience without attributing rhetorical preferences to a nationality or culture.
3. Plan an organizer, oral rehearsal and initial draft. Explain how the support serves this genre and how the writer retains responsibility for the composition.
4. Give focused, constructive feedback tied to the source and a relevant language feature. Describe the revision you would request, how the learner would explain the change, and how later editing would address selected conventions. Do not write the complete final answer for copying.
5. Preserve actual reading and development of connected written discourse after the oral entry. Distinguish the assisted revision from a later fresh opportunity to observe more independent writing.
6. State S11 Recommendation 3's Minimal evidence rating and its elementary/middle-school guide scope. Explain why the Strong ratings of other recommendations cannot be transferred to every writing scaffold. Identify an observation that would lead you to adjust support rather than promising a fixed effect or timeline.

This case samples the reading-writing link, genre, first-language resources and responsive process writing. It is not an official mentor-text assignment or a comprehensive writing progression.

tasks.title: Assess a wetland explanation for content and language
tasks.prompt:
Original unfamiliar non-math application. All people, observations and passages are synthetic. This is not an official examination item or official writing prompt. There is no deterministic answer key or keyword grading. The response remains needs_review and provisional/manual pending a real human judgment.

A grade 7 class is preparing a public explanation of how a wetland can influence water movement. The following original rehearsal passage is synthetic, not a published authentic scientific source:

'Water moving through the wetland encounters stems and uneven ground. In the shallow channel, the current slows and some suspended particles settle. However, a photograph of clearer water does not show whether dissolved substances remain. To evaluate a claim about water quality, investigators need evidence beyond appearance.'

The content target is to explain the described process and a limit of the available evidence. One learner points accurately to settling particles in a labeled model but writes, 'water slow particles down.' Another writes, 'The wetland removes every harmful substance because the water looks clear.' The second response uses a conventional sentence structure but makes a claim the passage does not establish. The class includes varied English domain profiles; none of these observations establishes a content-ability level or disability. A colleague wants to grade only grammar. Another suggests dropping the passage and accepting all oral explanations as full literacy mastery.

Plan and justify instruction and assessment:
1. State an observable content objective and a connected language objective for explaining a process and qualifying a claim. Name the Massachusetts content framework and WIDA standards as the two planning sources, but do not invent exact grade-standard wording absent from this packet.
2. Quote a demanding sentence, analyze a language relationship and identify needed background knowledge. Describe how you would select a real authentic content text for a classroom lesson and check that its claims align with the objective. Keep this synthetic passage's status explicit.
3. Choose meaningful chunking, a visual or first-language supplementary resource, and structured partner interaction. Require return to the full text rather than permanent replacement by a summary.
4. Explain what each learner's response shows and what it does not. Design a content-understanding probe distinct from a language-form check. Preserve the target and distinguish WIDA ELP from content ability.
5. Move from a whiteboard/oral entry to actual reading and a connected written explanation. Specify how feedback and a later writing opportunity develop discourse beyond a single copied sentence.
6. Identify evidence that would lead to concept reteaching, clause unpacking or reduced support. Record assistance and uncertainty; do not mark the scaffolded work as independent evidence or the objective as complete.

Use S1's content-area planning and access scope, S9's language development framework, S11's oral/written integration and S13's concurrent standards guidance. No grammar count or keyword list can evaluate the quality of this plan.

Review boundary: evaluate reasoning, quotations, support choices and uncertainty through a real human action. There is no single required plan or keyword list. Completion, unfamiliarity and a source_checked label do not establish independent evidence or mastery. Do not infer ability, disability or culture traits from English proficiency, language background or any isolated response.

tasks.title: Five-part original unofficial practice: How a community archive tells a story
tasks.prompt:
Original, unofficial five-part written-response practice, not an official MTEL prompt or assignment. This mentor passage and these prompts were authored for study; all town records and events are fictional. The public S2/S3 materials provide a sample for Part I only. Part I below mirrors that public analysis shape; Parts II-V are original, unofficial practice and do not reproduce or claim the official wording of live Parts II-V. Public reference: https://www.mtel.nesinc.com/Content/StudyGuide/MA_SG_CRI_56.asp.

Use the SAME mentor text, "How a community archive tells a story" (mentor.obj0013.community-archive), for all five parts. Identify it in Part I(a), keep its version/hash binding, and include literal quotes from that same mentor text in EVERY part. Do not switch passages. Quotes must support your analysis and decisions rather than decorate a generic plan. No prescribed word count or timing is imposed for this original practice.

This task uses the EXISTING rubric.mtel56.public@1: the verbatim public Purpose, Subject Matter Knowledge, Support and Rationale characteristics inform one holistic 1-4/U/B score. Apply U/B gates first; criterion comments are allowed, numeric per-criterion scores, weights and averages are not. Any review score is provisional and the reviewer is not the official MTEL scorer. Saving a submission creates an immutable attempt with no automatic independent evidence or score. Continue through the existing manual or Grok handoff packet/proposal workflow; no AI call is made here, and human review requires a real human action. Preserve the original answer.

parts.title: I. Mentor selection and analysis - original, unofficial practice
parts.prompt: Mirror the PUBLIC Part I task shape with this original mentor. (a) Identify the SAME mentor text, "How a community archive tells a story" (mentor.obj0013.community-archive), select the Secondary grade-level cluster and Social Science discipline with a grade 8 target for this original practice, and state a relevant content objective. (b) Select essential Tier One, Tier Two and Tier Three vocabulary that actually appears in the mentor; quote the selected words or phrases and justify each context-sensitive tier choice. (c) Identify sentence-level and discourse-level academic language features, quote their exact text, and explain how they make meaning. (d) State exactly three observable language objectives: vocabulary development and oracy, reading comprehension, and written discourse. Quote evidence from the SAME mentor text to justify each objective and connect it to the content objective. Do not substitute a different source or claim this is the official MTEL prompt.

parts.title: II. Vocabulary and oracy - original, unofficial practice
parts.prompt: Original, unofficial practice. Using the SAME mentor text, "How a community archive tells a story" (mentor.obj0013.community-archive), quote the words and a sentence that matter to your content objective. Plan a sequence that develops their meanings in context and gives partners a real reason to listen, ask for evidence and explain. Include familiar-language resources when useful without assuming identical literacy histories. Explain how you would check meaning beyond repetition and adjust supports for contrasting observed needs. All choices must be justified with literal quotes from the SAME mentor text.

parts.title: III. Reading supports - original, unofficial practice
parts.prompt: Original, unofficial practice. Quote a demanding sentence and a connected passage from the SAME mentor text, "How a community archive tells a story" (mentor.obj0013.community-archive). Analyze a possible decoding, language, background or strategic reading demand and describe an observation that would distinguish hypotheses. Plan a purposeful think-aloud, meaningful chunking or a visual/familiar-language support, then require reconnection and rereading of the original. Explain how the support preserves grade-level reasoning and how you would check comprehension rather than pronunciation alone. Use literal quotes from the SAME mentor text; an oral summary or permanently simplified replacement cannot substitute for the reading goal.

parts.title: IV. Writing supports - original, unofficial practice
parts.prompt: Original, unofficial practice. Quote evidence from the SAME mentor text, "How a community archive tells a story" (mentor.obj0013.community-archive), and plan a connected written explanation or museum label tied to your content objective. Connect source reading to planning, optional oral rehearsal, drafting, focused language/content feedback and revision. Explain a genre-appropriate organizer and how observed L1 writing resources could serve as a bridge without cultural assumptions. Show one feedback move without supplying the entire learner response. Require actual development of written discourse beyond talk or copying, and state that S11 Recommendation 3 has Minimal evidence rather than guaranteeing gains. Justify every major support with literal quotes from the SAME mentor text.

parts.title: V. Assessment and differentiation - original, unofficial practice
parts.prompt: Original, unofficial practice. Use literal quotes from the SAME mentor text, "How a community archive tells a story" (mentor.obj0013.community-archive), to design checks of content understanding and of the three language objectives. Specify evidence from listening, speaking, reading and writing and explain what each observation can and cannot show. Contrast a supported content claim expressed with emerging English and a grammatical but unsupported claim. Describe two evidence-based adjustments, how assistance is recorded, and a later fresh opportunity for more independent work. Differentiate access without lowering the content standard or inferring ability, disability or culture traits from ELP. Anchor the assessment decisions in quotes from the SAME mentor text and justify them; do not invent numeric criterion subscores or mark the objective complete.

cards.front: What should a teacher distinguish before selecting a reading support?
cards.back: Distinguish observed word-reading demands from language comprehension, background knowledge and strategic monitoring. These can interact. Use contrasting observations and text evidence; do not assume that every EL reading difficulty is phonics or infer ability from English proficiency.

cards.front: How do entry points differ for an L1-literate reader and a learner not yet literate in any language?
cards.back: Build on demonstrated L1 reading strategies and teach relevant English print/language differences for the L1-literate reader. Provide explicit initial literacy with an oral-language foundation for a learner not yet literate. Both need comprehension development and access to meaningful grade-level content.

cards.front: How can reading and writing support each other during revision?
cards.back: A draft can expose a misunderstanding or missing evidence. Reread the source, examine a quoted detail, give focused feedback on meaning and language, and ask the writer to revise and explain the change. Supported revision develops writing but is not unaided evidence.

cards.front: What evidence level belongs to Recommendation 3 in the 2014 WWC English-learner guide?
cards.back: Minimal. The guide recommends structured, content-anchored writing opportunities with language supports, collaboration and constructive feedback, while retaining this evidence limitation. Strong ratings for other recommendations do not transfer to every writing scaffold.

cards.front: How should Massachusetts content frameworks and WIDA standards work in a lesson?
cards.back: Plan a content objective and a language objective together: preserve disciplinary thinking while teaching the language needed to participate. Assess the supported content claim and how language communicates it; one objective does not replace the other.

cards.front: What makes chunking an access scaffold rather than permanent text replacement?
cards.back: Chunk the authentic content text at meaningful boundaries, add needed visual or first-language supports, then reconnect the chunks and return to the original. Check understanding of content relationships, not only English form. A permanently simplified sole text loses the original reading demand.

cards.front: What public-sample limit and mentor rule must five-part practice preserve?
cards.back: S2/S3 publish a Part I sample only. Authored Parts II-V must be labeled original, unofficial practice. Identify one mentor in Part I(a) and use that same mentor throughout; quote its evidence to justify the analysis and instructional choices.

cards.front: How do criterion comments differ from the public holistic score?
cards.back: Purpose, Subject Matter Knowledge, Support and Rationale inform one holistic 1-4/U/B judgment. Apply U/B gates first. Comments may cite response evidence and gaps; numeric per-criterion subscores or invented weights are not the official rubric. Any practice review score stays provisional.

mentorTexts.title: How a community archive tells a story
mentorTexts.text:
A community archive preserves records that people can use to investigate the past. Its collection may include letters, maps, photographs, meeting notes, and recorded recollections. A primary source was created by someone who experienced or took part in an event or period being studied. Such a source offers evidence from a particular position; it is not a complete account of everything that happened.

In the fictional town of Alder Crossing, students investigate why a public reading room moved from a shop to a larger building. A committee's meeting notes state that the shop had little space for books. A letter from a reader describes difficulty reaching the shop after the evening bus stopped running. Although the notes and letter concern the same reading room, they emphasize different problems. The notes explain a concern discussed by the committee, while the letter records one reader's experience.

The students compare the records before writing a museum label. They can support the claim that limited space concerned the committee and that transportation concerned at least one reader. However, the letter alone cannot show that every reader had the same experience. A photograph of the new building shows its entrance and windows, but it does not explain why the move was approved. To investigate the decision further, the students would need additional records, such as the committee's final explanation.

An archive can therefore help a community examine change without supplying a single unquestionable story. Researchers identify who created each record, consider its purpose, and compare its details with other evidence. When a record leaves a question unanswered, a careful explanation names the uncertainty instead of filling the gap with an invented fact. Preserving different voices makes more questions possible; comparing those voices helps researchers judge what each claim can support.
